title: Trapezoidal Irrigation Canal: Normal Depth & Manning's Design
description:
A concrete-lined trapezoidal irrigation canal (Manning's n = 0.013) must carry Q = 120 cfs on a slope S₀ = 0.0003 ft/ft. The channel has a bottom width b = 8 ft and side slopes z = 1.5H:1V (1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical).

Using Manning's equation:
Q = (1.49/n) · A · R^(2/3) · S₀^(1/2)

Where:
• A = (b + zy)·y  (flow area)
• P = b + 2y·√(1 + z²)  (wetted perimeter)
• R = A/P  (hydraulic radius)

Determine:
1. The normal depth yₙ (ft) that satisfies Manning's equation
2. The critical depth yc (ft) where the Froude number equals 1.0
3. Whether the flow is subcritical or supercritical at normal depth
4. The Froude number at normal depth

The normal depth and flow regime are most nearly:
hint: Solve Manning's equation iteratively (bisection): find yₙ such that Q_Manning(yₙ) = Q_design. Critical depth is where Fr = 1, i.e., Q²T = gA³.
shortcut: For mild slopes (S₀ < Sc), the channel is on a mild grade and normal flow is always subcritical (yₙ > yc). You only need to check if the slope exceeds Sc = g·n²/(1.49²·R^(1/3)) to classify the slope.
fifthGrader: Imagine water sliding down a very gentle ramp. It moves slowly and deep (subcritical). If the ramp were steeper, the water would zoom fast and thin (supercritical). Normal depth is just how deep the water settles at whatever speed matches the slope!

title: Hydraulic Jump: Conjugate Depth & Energy Loss in Rectangular Channel
description:
Water flows at Q = 80 cfs in a rectangular concrete channel (b = 5 ft wide, n = 0.013). Supercritical flow enters at an upstream depth y₁ = 0.65 ft after a spillway.

A hydraulic jump forms, transitioning to subcritical flow downstream. Using the momentum equation for a rectangular channel:

y₂/y₁ = (1/2)·(-1 + √(1 + 8·Fr₁²))

Where Fr₁ = V₁/√(g·y₁) is the upstream Froude number.

The energy loss through the jump:
ΔE = (y₂ - y₁)³ / (4·y₁·y₂)

Determine:
1. The upstream Froude number Fr₁
2. The conjugate (sequent) depth y₂ downstream of the jump
3. The head loss ΔE through the hydraulic jump (ft)
4. The percentage of upstream specific energy dissipated

The conjugate depth and head loss are most nearly:
hint: Step 1: V₁ = Q/(b·y₁). Step 2: Fr₁ = V₁/√(g·y₁). Step 3: Conjugate depth y₂ = (y₁/2)·(-1 + √(1+8Fr₁²)). Step 4: ΔE = (y₂-y₁)³/(4y₁y₂).
shortcut: For a strong jump (Fr₁ > 4.5), the energy loss exceeds 45% — very effective energy dissipation. The ratio y₂/y₁ is always greater than 1 and increases rapidly with Fr₁. Memorize: at Fr₁ = 3, y₂ ≈ 3.77·y₁.
fifthGrader: A hydraulic jump is like when you step in a puddle really fast — the water splashes up and slows down! Fast shallow water suddenly becomes slow deep water. All that crashing and splashing loses energy, which is exactly what engineers want below a dam to protect the riverbed!

title: Specific Energy & Critical Slope Classification
description:
A trapezoidal channel (b = 6 ft, z = 2H:1V) carries Q = 90 cfs with Manning's n = 0.025 (earth lining). The design depth is y = 2.5 ft.

Specific energy (total head referenced to channel bottom):
E = y + V²/(2g) = y + Q²/(2g·A²)

Critical slope (the slope at which normal depth = critical depth):
Sc = g·n²·A / (1.49²·R^(1/3)·T)  [US customary]

For the given flow conditions, determine:
1. The specific energy E at the design depth (ft)
2. The critical depth yc and minimum specific energy Emin
3. The critical slope Sc for this channel geometry
4. Classify the channel slope (mild/critical/steep) for S₀ = 0.001 ft/ft
5. The Froude number at design depth

The specific energy and critical slope are most nearly:
hint: E = y + Q²/(2gA²). For critical depth, solve Q²T = gA³ iteratively. Critical slope Sc is the slope where Manning's equation gives yn = yc. If S₀ < Sc, channel is mild (M-curve); if S₀ > Sc, channel is steep (S-curve).
shortcut: Quick check: compute Fr at the design depth. If Fr < 1, you're subcritical. Critical slope is typically 0.003–0.012 for concrete channels and 0.001–0.005 for earthen channels at moderate flows.
fifthGrader: Specific energy is like how much 'oomph' the water has — some comes from how deep it is, and some from how fast it's moving. Every amount of water can flow at two different depths with the same energy — one deep and slow, one shallow and fast. The critical depth is the middle ground where it uses the least oomph!

title: Natural Stream Flow: Manning's n Selection & Regime Classification
description:
A natural stream channel has an approximately trapezoidal cross-section with b = 12 ft, side slopes z = 2H:1V, and a longitudinal slope S₀ = 0.0015 ft/ft. The stream has moderate irregularity, some weeds, and a few scattered boulders.

From ASCE/Chow Table of Manning's n values:
• Clean straight channel: n = 0.030
• Minor irregularities: +0.005
• Some vegetation (weeds): +0.005–0.010
• Obstructions (boulders): +0.005

For a bankfull discharge Q = 350 cfs, determine:
1. The appropriate Manning's n (composite value)
2. The normal depth yₙ at bankfull flow
3. The critical depth yc
4. Flow regime (subcritical or supercritical) at normal depth
5. The average channel velocity (ft/s)

The bankfull normal depth and Froude number are most nearly:
hint: Select n = 0.030 base + 0.005 (irregularity) + 0.008 (weeds) + 0.005 (boulders) = 0.048. Then solve Manning's for yn. Most natural streams on S₀ ≈ 0.001 are subcritical (mild slope).
shortcut: Natural channels almost always have mild slopes (S₀ < Sc) and subcritical flow. Steep slopes with supercritical flow are typically only found in mountain streams or engineered spillway chutes.
fifthGrader: Imagine the stream bed is like a carpet. A smooth tile floor lets you slide fast (low n). Shaggy carpet with rocks everywhere slows you down (high n). Manning's n is the stream's 'roughness score' — the higher it is, the slower the water moves for the same slope!
